newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- APRIL 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- APRIL 17.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--Greece is slowly moving into a period of industrial growth, expected to be further boosted by structural changes to come out of the government's "social dialogue" with unions and employers. Industrialists yesterday called for the government's support for the offensive by Greek capital both domestically and abroad.

--National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou yesterday wrangled an agreement from US Commerce Secretary William Daloy that Greece coordinate initiatives to attract US capital to southern European countries such as Albania, Bulgaria and the Black Sea states. Papandoniou said Greece had the infrastructure to support US investment in these countries and could act as a base for US firms' expansion.

--The Federation of Greek Industries (SEV) yesterday added their criticism of the government's proposals to constitute the agenda for "social dialogue" saying the planned tool for the resolution of the country's infrastructural problems was in danger of becoming a forum of endless talk. The government's 19-point proposal is "unclear and timid", the SEV vice-president said.

--The Greek economy will get its regular check-up from the European Union, OECD and the International Monetary Fund in the next two months, in reports that will be decisive for the government's planning and movements on meeting convergence criteria in time.
--SEV has called for the activation of the competition committee to mediate conflicts between industrialists and retailers.

--National Westminister's books in Greece are being closely examined by the tax department, sources say. The finance ministry is reportedly seriously concerned at irregularities found in the audit so far.
--Increased tariffs and rates for public utilities and organisations (DEKOs) will be introduced in the second half 1997. The increases are expected to be close to expected inflation levels.
--Some 35 per cent of Greek firms have credit problems, according to a recent ICAP survey.

--A new finance ministry measure will see fines for the non-payment of Value Added Tax reduced as well as a series of new punitive measures for tax evasion within the year. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
